about.title: Blythe Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Blythe sits along the I-10 corridor, a heavily traveled route for freight, agriculture, and service industries that make up much of the local economy. Workers in trucking, warehousing, roadside maintenance, and retail near W Hobson Way face real risks every shift, from equipment accidents to vehicle-related injuries on the job. In California, workers' compensation usually covers medical costs and lost wages regardless of fault, but it doesn't allow you to sue your employer. When a negligent third party is involved, like a subcontractor, equipment manufacturer, property owner, or another driver, you may have a separate legal path to pursue additional compensation. LawProactive doesn't practice law; we simply connect injured workers in Blythe with an independent attorney from our network who can review the details of your accident and explain what options may apply, including whether a third-party claim makes sense alongside any workers' comp benefits you're already receiving.

whyChoose.title: Why Blythe Workers Turn to LawProactive

items.title: Understanding Your Exclusive Remedy Limits
items.desc: California workers' comp is typically the exclusive remedy against your employer, but that doesn't mean it's your only option. An attorney can help identify whether a third party's negligence contributed to your injury.

items.title: Protection Against Retaliation
items.desc: Reporting a workplace injury to your employer within 30 days is required under California law, and retaliation for doing so is illegal. If you're worried about your job after an injury, an attorney can explain your rights.

items.title: Navigating the Two-Year Deadline
items.desc: Third-party injury claims in California carry a two-year statute of limitations. Getting connected with an attorney early helps ensure evidence and deadlines aren't missed while you focus on recovery.

items.question: I already filed a workers' comp claim in Blythe. Can I still pursue something else?
items.answer: Yes, in many cases. Workers' comp and a third-party claim aren't mutually exclusive if someone other than your employer contributed to your injury, such as a subcontractor or another driver on I-10. An independent attorney can review your situation and explain whether a separate claim applies.

items.question: What if my employer says I waited too long to report my injury?
items.answer: California generally requires you to report a workplace injury to your employer within 30 days. If there's a dispute about timing, an attorney in our network can look at the specifics of your case and advise you on next steps.

items.question: Does LawProactive charge anything to connect me with an attorney?
items.answer: No, our connection service is completely free. Attorneys in our network typically work on contingency, meaning they only get paid if you recover compensation.
